{{nihongo|'''Jun-ichi Igusa'''|井草 凖一|Igusa Jun’ichi|30 January 1924 – 24 November 2013}} was a Japanese [[mathematician]] who for over three decades was on the faculty at [[Johns Hopkins University]]. He is known for his contributions to [[algebraic geometry]] and [[number theory]]. The [[Igusa zeta-function]], the [[Igusa quartic]], [[Igusa subgroup]]s, [[Igusa curve]]s, and [[Igusa varieties]] are named after him.<ref name="jhuobit"/>

He was an invited speaker for the 1962 [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in [[Stockholm]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.mathunion.org/db/ICM/Speakers/SortedByLastname.php |title=International Mathematical Union (IMU) |website=www.mathunion.org |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927014538/http://www.mathunion.org/db/ICM/Speakers/SortedByLastname.php |archive-date=2011-09-27}}</ref> He was awarded Japan's [[Order of the Sacred Treasure]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Mathematician Receives Japan's Order of the Sacred Treasure |url=https://pages.jh.edu/news_info/news/home05/jan05/math.html |access-date=17 October 2019 |publisher=Johns Hopkins University |date=5 January 2005 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050404154437/http://www.jhu.edu/news/home05/jan05/math.html |archive-date=4 April 2005}}</ref> In 2012 he became a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved 2013-01-26.</ref>

==Life and career==
Igusa was born in Kiyosato village, [[Gunma Prefecture]], Japan, on 30 January 1924.<ref>{{cite book |last=Lo |first=Samuel E. |year=1971 |title=Asian Who? in America |publisher=East-West Who |page=109 }}</ref> He graduated from the [[University of Tokyo]] in 1945 and received his [[Ph.D.]] from [[Kyoto University]] in 1953, after which he became professor of mathematics at the [[University of Tsukuba]]. After a brief period spent at [[Harvard University]], he took up a permanent position at Johns Hopkins University, in [[Baltimore]]. Igusa taught at Johns Hopkins from 1955 to 1993.<ref name="bsunobit">{{cite news |last1=Kelly |first1=Jacques |title=Jun-ichi Igusa |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2013/12/09/jun-ichi-igusa/ |access-date=17 October 2019 |work=Baltimore Sun |date=6 December 2013}}</ref> He joined the staff of the ''[[American Journal of Mathematics]]'' as an associate editor in 1964, and served as chief editor between 1978 and 1993.<ref>{{cite journal |title=In Memoriam: Jun-Ichi Igusa 1924–2013 |journal=American Journal of Mathematics |date=February 2014 |volume=136 |issue=1 |page=iii |doi=10.1353/ajm.2014.0000 |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/article/535939|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Igusa died, aged 89, of a stroke at Holly Hill Nursing Home in [[Towson, Maryland]], on 24 November 2013.<ref name="bsunobit"/>

He had three sons, Kiyoshi, Takeru and Mitsuru.<ref name="jhuobit">{{cite news |url=https://hub.jhu.edu/2013/12/02/jun-ichi-igusa-mathematics/ |access-date=2013-11-29 |url-status=live |publisher=Johns Hopkins University |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203001813/http://krieger.jhu.edu/blog/2013/11/27/jun-ichi-igusa-noted-mathematician-and-researcher-died-at-89/ |archive-date=2013-12-03 |title=Jun-ichi Igusa, noted mathematician and JHU researcher, dies at 89}}</ref> Takeru Igusa is a professor of civil engineering at [[Johns Hopkins University]]. [[Kiyoshi Igusa]] is a professor of mathematics at [[Brandeis University]].
